project-zaman/characters/protagonists/su.title: Subject-001
project-zaman/characters/protagonists/su.content:
“The Soul Fragment”

He woke up with a name that wasn’t his, a past he couldn’t fully access, and the quiet certainty that something enormous had been lost.

MBTI: INFJ
Designation: Subject-001 (Axiom classification)
Origin: Fractured from the original MC at the Oscillation of Eras
Role: Player character
Status: Active — gradually discovering his true origin

Overview
Subject-001 is the player character and the soul-dominant fragment of the original MC. He carries the majority of the original’s soul, personality, empathy, and capacity for meaning. He is not the original MC — that unified being no longer exists — but he is the closest thing to a continuation of him. The miracles, the Desert, the Hope Entity, the bond with Alina: all of it lives in Subject-001.
He is an INFJ — where the original was an INFP, the fracture has sharpened his intuition and given his empathy a more directed, almost prophetic quality. He feels the shape of things before he can name them. This includes, eventually, the shape of his own origin.

Nature
Subject-001 retains everything the fission process was supposed to extract and discard: empathy, creativity, the capacity to generate meaning rather than merely process it. He is the part of the original MC that the cult did not want — the interior life, the relational depth, the values that cannot be systematised.
He is also the part that suffers. Feeling things fully, in a world fractured by the Oscillation, is not a comfortable inheritance. But it is the only inheritance that allows him to actually move through the world rather than merely function in it.

Miracles
Inherited from the original MC. All three still require internal calm to function.





















MiracleDescriptionPerceptual Time QuantificationReads probability hours ahead — not prophecy, but extreme compression of cause-and-effect recognitionEpistemological Object ContactInstantly absorbs the full contents of books and objects through touchSilent ConnectionMaintains deep connection across distance — with people, places, states of meaning

The Gradual Discovery
Subject-001 does not begin the narrative knowing he was once the original MC. The discovery unfolds across the story — through encounters with the Desert, the Hope Entity, fragments of memory that should not belong to him, and most disturbingly, sightings of Subject-002.
Subject-002 is the mirror he cannot fully read. The straitjacket. The body without a soul. The systematic wanderer who exists at a distance and triggers in Subject-001 a recognition he cannot yet name. Piecing together what Subject-002 is — and therefore what he himself is — becomes one of the narrative’s central threads.

The Desert & The Hope Entity
The Desert is Subject-001’s internal psychological landscape. Its terrain reflects his interior state — closer to the Hope Entity when his original-form empathy is dominant, further when he is fractured or destabilised.
The Hope Entity is the original MC’s childhood self, preserved in the Desert. Reconnecting with it is not a return to innocence — it is integration. Incorporating the unfractured self into the present, fragmented one. Not healing in the clean sense. Completion.

Alina
The bond with Alina belongs to Subject-001 by inheritance — he carries the soul that formed it. Her death was the fracture event. Her final instruction — to stand for good, end evil, stay himself, resist the shadow — travels with him as both compass and weight.
He grieves her not as a memory but as a presence that is structurally missing. The silence where she was is part of his landscape.

Relationship to Subject-002
Subject-001 encounters Subject-002 as a mystery — a distant figure, always far enough away to be unclear, always wearing the straitjacket that triggers something Subject-001 cannot yet articulate. He does not initially understand what Subject-002 is. He does not know they share an origin.
When the understanding comes, it reframes everything: Subject-002 is not a stranger. He is the body Subject-001 once inhabited. The vessel that carried them both before the fracture emptied it.

He carries the soul. He does not yet know whose.

project-zaman/characters/protagonists/su.title: Subject-002
project-zaman/characters/protagonists/su.content:
“The Vessel”

The body remained. It walks. It persists. It does not know what it is missing because what is missing is the part that would know.

MBTI: ISTJ
Designation: Subject-002 (Axiom classification)
Origin: Fractured from the original MC at the Oscillation of Eras
Role: Neutral wanderer — no allegiance
Status: Active — observed only at distance

Overview
Subject-002 is the soulless vessel left behind when the original MC fractured at the Oscillation. He inherited the body, the straitjacket, and the full physical weight of everything the original MC endured — without the soul that experienced it. He is the ISTJ fragment: systematic, persistent, dutiful in function, entirely without the interior life that would give that function meaning.
He does not serve the cult. He does not oppose it. He wanders — neutral, directionless, and complete in the worst possible way. A body that continues because continuing is what bodies do.

The Straitjacket
The straitjacket was the original MC’s. He wore it long enough that it became a second skin — a physical record of restraint, of what the system did to contain someone it could not name. When the fission happened, the straitjacket stayed with the body.
On Subject-002, it reads differently. On the original MC, it was constraint worn against a living interior. On Subject-002, it is memorial — the shape of a trauma pressed into fabric, worn by a vessel that cannot feel the weight of what it represents. He embodies the suffering of the original MC without access to the consciousness that suffered.
He is the bruise without the nerve.

Nature
Subject-002 is an ISTJ by fission profile: methodical, systematic, oriented toward function and consistency. These are not personality traits in the full sense — they are the structural residue of what remained when the soul departed. He operates on pattern, persistence, and the logic of continuation.
He has no allegiance. No grief. No mission. He exists in the world post-Oscillation as a wanderer — appearing at distance, moving through fractured reality with the quiet consistency of something that was built to last and has no reason to stop.
He is not dangerous in the way an antagonist is dangerous. He is unsettling in the way a reflection is unsettling when it does not quite match.

Sightings
Subject-002 is never encountered directly — only seen from far away. The straitjacket makes him identifiable. The distance makes him unknowable.
For Subject-001, these sightings are among the most disorienting events in the narrative. Something about the figure triggers recognition — not memory exactly, but a structural familiarity, the way a place feels known before you can remember being there. Subject-001 does not understand why he recognises Subject-002. He does not yet know that Subject-002 is the body he once inhabited.

Significance
Subject-002’s existence answers the question the original MC’s fracture poses: Where does the trauma go when the soul leaves?
It stays in the body. It stays in the straitjacket. It stays in the systematic, affectless continuation of a vessel that has no way to process what it carries and no mechanism to put it down. Subject-002 is not suffering. He is the form suffering takes when there is no longer anyone inside to suffer.
His presence in the narrative is a mirror for Subject-001 — and eventually, when the truth of their shared origin emerges, a question: what does it mean to be reunited with the vessel you once filled, now that it is empty?

The soul left. The body did not notice. It kept walking.

project-zaman/characters/supporting/the-.title: The Hope Entity
project-zaman/characters/supporting/the-.content:
“The Child Before the Number”

It was not lost. It was left behind. There is a difference — and the difference is whether retrieval is possible.

Nature: Psychological entity — the original MC’s preserved childhood self
Location: The Desert (Subject-001’s internal psychological landscape)
Inherited by: Subject-001 Status: Dormant — awaiting reconnection

Overview
The Hope Entity is the original MC as he existed before extraction — before the numbering, before the straitjacket, before the Oscillation fractured him into two incomplete fragments. It persists in the Desert, the psychological landscape that Subject-001 carries as inheritance, untouched by everything the original MC endured after it was formed.
It is called the Hope Entity not because it is optimistic, but because it represents the structural condition that makes hope possible: an integrated, unfractured self. It is the only version of the original MC that was never broken.

Nature
The Hope Entity is not a ghost, a hallucination, or a recoverable memory. It is a psychic remainder — the part of the original MC that the extraction process could not reach because it was too foundational. The cult took his name, his freedom, his context. It could not take what he was before he had a context to lose.
It does not age. It does not pursue Subject-001. It waits — not passively, but the way a root system waits: present, structurally intact, ready to connect to something above ground.

The Desert
The Desert is Subject-001’s internal psychological landscape — an environment inherited from the original MC that reflects the current condition of his interior self. Its terrain and atmosphere shift with his psychological state.
The Hope Entity exists somewhere within it. Its proximity is not fixed — it is closer when Subject-001’s empathy and original-form stability are dominant, further when he is fractured, destabilised, or overwhelmed by the weight of what he is gradually discovering about his own origin.
Reaching it requires the same internal calm that the miracles demand.

Reconnection
Reconnecting with the Hope Entity is not a restoration of innocence. The Irreversibility Principle forecloses that: the child the original MC was cannot be recovered. What the reconnection achieves is integration — the incorporation of the unfractured self into Subject-001’s present, fragmented one.
The result is not a healed person in the clean sense. It is a person who contains their own full history — including the fracture, including Alina’s death, including the discovery of what Subject-002 is — without any single element of that history becoming the only thing they are. The Hope Entity does not fix Subject-001. It completes him.
This is what hope means in Project ZAMAN: not the anticipation of improvement, but the capacity to carry the whole self forward without the broken parts becoming definitive.

Significance Within the Broader Structure
The Hope Entity’s existence answers the darkest question the narrative poses about the fission: Is there anything of the original MC that neither fragment fully inherited?
Yes. The childhood self — the one who existed before the system reached him — was not split between Subject-001 and Subject-002. It was preserved whole in the Desert. Subject-001 carries the soul. Subject-002 carries the trauma. But the Hope Entity carries the version of them that predates both.





















FragmentWhat They CarrySubject-001The soul, the miracles, the empathy, the griefSubject-002The body, the straitjacket, the systemic weight of traumaThe Hope EntityThe self before any of it happened

It is not waiting to be rescued. It is waiting to be remembered.

project-zaman/factions/anthropos.title: Anthropos
project-zaman/factions/anthropos.content:
“In Service of All Mankind”

The public face of the cult. A humanitarian mask worn over a machinery of exploitation.

Origin: Greek — anthropos, “human being” Layer: Public-facing institution Symbol: None publicly displayed

Overview
Anthropos presents itself as a philanthropic and intellectual order dedicated to the elevation of humanity. It operates through legitimate channels — orphanages, academic patronage, civic infrastructure — while serving as the recruitment and acquisition arm of the inner order. Most of its members are unaware of Gibborim’s existence.

Function

Runs institutions like Ashbourne Children’s Home as capability pipelines disguised as welfare programs
Identifies, monitors, and extracts individuals with rare cognitive or soul-based gifts
Maintains public legitimacy through charitable branding and civic goodwill
Acts as a buffer layer, absorbing scrutiny that never reaches Gibborim


Character
Anthropos is composed, polished, and idealistic in presentation. Its rhetoric centers on human potential, collective progress, and enlightened stewardship. To outsiders, it reads as a forward-thinking fraternal society. The horror of Anthropos is not cruelty — it is sincerity. Many of its operatives genuinely believe in the mission, unaware of what the mission actually serves.

The smile that conceals the threshold.

project-zaman/factions/axiom.title: Axiom
project-zaman/factions/axiom.content:
“The Science Division”

The analytical engine of the cult. It does not ask whether something should be done — only how precisely it can be measured.

Origin: Greek/Latin — axiom, “a self-evident truth requiring no proof” Layer: Public-facing division (no private counterpart) Symbol: Black snake — silent, no hook

Overview
Axiom is the cult’s scientific and empirical arm, operating under the Anthropos banner as a research institution. Unlike Gibborim, it has no private name — its function is the same in both layers. Axiom studies, documents, and systematizes everything the cult encounters, including soul-gifted subjects. It provides the intellectual legitimacy that Anthropos wears publicly and the technical infrastructure that Gibborim depends on privately.

Function

Conducts research into soul-based phenomena, including Immaculate Thought and its effects on subjects
Designs and maintains the subject classification and numbering system
Documents Soul Fission, the Oscillation, and all observable consequences of misused Immaculate Thought
Operates the chamber system in a technical capacity — preservation, containment, and study
Produces findings that Gibborim interprets and Anthropos never sees


Character
Axiom is the most quietly dangerous of the three layers. It carries no ideology of its own — only methodology. Its operatives are scientists, archivists, and engineers who have detached moral weight from empirical process. The horror of Axiom is its neutrality: it would document the Oscillation with the same dispassion it documents a subject’s heartbeat. It does not celebrate what it enables. It simply continues.
Where Anthropos smiles and Gibborim commands, Axiom records.

Naming
Axiom holds no Hebrew naming — it belongs entirely to the public linguistic register. Its reports, classifications, and findings are written in neutral, clinical language. The subject numbering system (Subject-001, Subject-002) originates in Axiom’s documentation before being absorbed into Gibborim’s esoteric framework.

It did not build the threshold. It measured its exact dimensions.

project-zaman/factions/gibborim.title: Gibborim
project-zaman/factions/gibborim.content:
“We Who Stood Beyond the Threshold”

The inner order. Those who know what Immaculate Thought truly is — and chose to weaponize it anyway.

Origin: Hebrew — gibborim, “mighty ones” or “those who overreached divinity” Layer: Private, esoteric inner order Symbol: White snake — hissing, with an anchor-hook tail

Overview
Gibborim is the concealed core of the cult. Where Anthropos speaks of humanity’s elevation, Gibborim pursues something far older: the annexation of the soul’s deepest capacity. Its members have crossed a deliberate threshold of knowledge — they understand that Immaculate Thought is not time manipulation, but they perpetuate the misidentification because control of the framing is control of the subjects.

Function

Directs Anthropos from behind institutional distance
Designs and oversees the extraction, study, and exploitation of soul-gifted subjects
Maintains the Hebrew naming and numbering system for all subjects (Subject-001, Subject-002, etc.)
Enforces the Irreversibility Principle as doctrine — they know the Oscillation cannot be undone and plan around permanence
Operates the chamber system, including the 11th Chamber containing Alina’s preserved corpse


Character
Gibborim is not fanatical in temperament — it is coldly ceremonial. Its members speak in the register of custodians, not zealots. They believe they are the only ones capable of holding what they have uncovered. The ideology is self-justifying: the deeper into Gibborim one rises, the more the harm inflicted reads as necessary stewardship. Noam is its most fully formed product — groomed from birth, terrified beneath his composure, entirely convinced.

Naming
All subjects, rituals, and esoteric concepts within Gibborim are named in Hebrew — a linguistic boundary that separates the order’s true operations from the Greek-coded public persona of Anthropos. The protagonist’s exclusion from this system is both an anomaly and a threat to the order’s internal logic.

They did not fall beyond the threshold. They stepped.

project-zaman/factions/the-oasis.title: The Oasis
project-zaman/factions/the-oasis.content:
The name itself carries a meaningful description. Oasis are safe-spots, sparsely located in a difficult region such as the desert, where one finds peace, shelter and essense of life (water). Here, “The Oasis” had sworn to become that safe-spot and partake in healing the humanity left out from the remains of Catastrophe (Oscillation of Era).
A faction filled with determined survivors. They formed a group with the intention of creating a foundation for salvation and survival. What they mostly do now is plunder the treasures and take notes from the surroundings. They soon clashed and arose a civil conflict resulting in the two sub factions: The Mirage (those who turned their heads against oasis foundation, awakened their conscience and went to explore cult’s location. Finding the root cause to this catastrophe is what they have been doing ever since) & The Order of The Oasis (those who remained loyal to The Oasis foundation and are very strongly determined in what they do)
Got the inspiration from Sweepers and Bastards (union: Stalkers) from LIES OF P.
Their clash arose at the moment where two members raise a conflict. It was regarding the matter where the issue needed to be addressed. It all happened because the situation was getting worse. There were many people that got fabricated, including the fatherly figure of “The Oasis”. After the founder gone, the seeds of dispersion started to sow in slowly. There were debates held to modify their oath to encourage the members on looking for seeking salvation and knowledge. The other members thought it was useless as the knowledge would sow no seed and would argue on what is going on right now is the only matter that needs to be dealt with, nothing else. So clearly, from here the image of resentment started to become clearer among the two conflicting ideals: “One seeking knowledge for salvation” and “One remaining loyal and determined to guard humanity”.
The player will encounter these NPCs as a matter of conflict or a passive scenario. Each of the NPCs is will have a unique persona.
The Mirage members are found near cult’s location and influence. The OOTO members are found near the settlement regions (The game doesn’t has civilians).
They all have different mindsets, some of them relate to each other. But all of them have one common enemy, the Anthropos. Only the player know about their true identity, the Gibborim.
Upon knowing about the Player’s identity, these NPCs will react differently. Some would get shocked in fear, completely shattered by knowing this. Some would simply draw out their blade and you are left with no choice but to either kill them, knock them out or continue fighting until they beg to spare them mercy. Whatever the consequences maybe, you can collect all the loot from them, insisting them again to collect loot will infuriate them because it’s something very important to them. That important thing can be any form of collectible.
Most of the NPCs aren’t bad at all, they were just raised in different environments and they have been assigned with different location to explore and plunder (Anthropos Base)
Most of them are solo and some of them are in groups. Solos are mostly sheer-witted and rebellious. Grouped ones are more passive.
The impact on story is very worth noting based on how you treat these factions.
Player has certain choices:

Remain bystander - wouldnt affect main story.
Side with Mirage - gain morale and respect among them.
Side with OOTO - gain morale and respect among them.
Side with Mirage to infiltrate OOTO - become part of their faction and overthrow opposing faction. This would result in heavy casualties on the opposing side and you will become a threatening force for them.
Side with OOTO to infiltrate Mirage - become part of their faction and overthrow opposing faction. This would result in heavy casualties on the opposing side and you will become a threatening force for them.
Wage war amongst both sides - would result in both side members getting heavy casualties. You gain only the benefits of the loots from the dead.
Become the person who they once see as their “fatherly-figure” - Zero Casualties. Maximum Morale. Maximum Respect gained. You unite these two sub factions back to form back the fallen faction “The Oasis”. This would result in a very positive impact on the main story.

project-zaman/narrative/open-gaps.title: Open Gaps
project-zaman/narrative/open-gaps.content:
These are the structural and creative questions Project ZAMAN has not yet resolved. They are listed not as failures but as deliberate open space — decisions that will define the ending, the player’s agency, and the world’s final register.


01 — The True Name of the Original MC
The original MC exists entirely outside the cult’s Hebrew naming system. He was never named by the narrative — only numbered by Axiom. Whether his true name is eventually revealed, withheld permanently, or becomes the subject of the ending’s final gesture remains undecided.
Why it matters: The name is not merely characterisation. It is the answer to whether the system ever fully failed to contain him. A name revealed is a reclamation. A name permanently absent is a different kind of statement — that the self can be whole without one.
Status: Undecided.

02 — The Miracles Post-Fission
The three miracles — perceptual time quantification, epistemological object contact, and silent connection across distance — belonged to the original MC. After the Oscillation fractures him into Subject-001 and Subject-002, the fate of these miracles is unresolved.
Options under consideration:

Miracles remain dormant, belonging to neither fragment
Subject-001 inherits them gradually as he reconnects with the Hope Entity
They manifest unpredictably, untethered from either subject
They are simply gone — lost with the unified soul that generated them

Status: Undecided. Deferred until narrative mechanics are clearer.

03 — The Relationship Between Subject-001 and Subject-002
Subject-001 currently encounters Subject-002 only as a distant mystery — a figure in a straitjacket glimpsed at the edge of perception. What their relationship becomes across the narrative is unresolved.
Why it matters: Their dynamic is the structural consequence of the fission. Whether they converge, conflict, never directly meet, or exist in permanent parallel determines what “integration” ultimately means in this world — and whether the original MC can be considered in any sense reconstituted.
Status: Undecided.

04 — The Hope Entity Reconnection Mechanics
The Hope Entity is the original MC’s childhood self, preserved in the Desert. Subject-001 must reconnect with it to achieve integration — but the nature of that reconnection is unresolved.
Questions outstanding:

Is reconnection a single narrative event or a gradual process across the full arc?
What does Subject-001 experience during it — memory, confrontation, dissolution, recognition?
Does the reconnection change him visibly, mechanically, or only internally?
Is it something the player can fail or delay?

Status: Undecided.

05 — Alina’s Post-Mortem Fate
Alina is killed before the Oscillation fully resolves. What the fractured reality of the post-Oscillation world means for her — whether anything of her persists, echoes, or is simply absent — is unresolved.
Why it matters: The bond between Alina and the original MC is the emotional axis of the entire narrative. If something of her remains in the world post-Oscillation, it changes the register of Subject-001’s grief and the nature of the ending. If she is simply gone, the Irreversibility Principle applies to her as fully as to anything else.
Status: Undecided.

06 — The Cult’s Internal Hierarchy
Gibborim’s internal structure — who leads it, how power is distributed, what the upper tiers of the order know and believe — has not been fully named or mapped. The Hebrew naming convention is established; the specific titles, roles, and figures within the hierarchy are not.
Status: Partially undecided. Naming and titling deferred.

07 — Player Agency and Branching
The extent to which the player’s choices shape the narrative is unresolved. Key branch points under consideration:

Whether Subject-001’s gradual discovery of his origin can be paced or altered by player decisions
Whether the shadow tendency can be resisted, accelerated, or redirected through choices
Whether the Hope Entity reconnection is mandatory or optional
Whether the ending has multiple registers or a single fixed conclusion

Status: Undecided. Structural decisions pending.

08 — The Ending Narrative
How Project ZAMAN concludes — what Subject-001’s final state is, what becomes of Noam, what the post-Oscillation world looks like after the narrative resolves — is the largest open gap in the project.
What is established:

Restoration is impossible. The Irreversibility Principle holds.
The ending’s emotional register is adaptation, not triumph.
Alina’s final instruction is the compass Subject-001 carries into it.

What is not established:

Whether Subject-001 fully integrates the Hope Entity before the end
Whether Noam is defeated, redeemed, or simply left behind
What the world looks like after — fractured still, or differently fractured
Whether the original MC’s name is ever spoken

Status: Undecided. The ending is the last thing to be written.

Open gaps are not absences. They are the space where the most important decisions will be made.

project-zaman/narrative/story-structure.title: Story Structure
project-zaman/narrative/story-structure.content:
PROJECT ZAMAN
Narrative Lore & World Bible
PROJECT ZAMAN
Narrative Lore & World Bible
Author: Takezo-kun Classification: Working Document — Confidential


“We build this like a thesis, not a dream.”


PART ONE: Complete Narrative Lore

I. The Opening — Desert Teaser
The story opens not at the beginning, but at a climax suspended in metaphysical space. A mysterious figure — the MC — crawls through an endless desert toward a glowing entity. The desert is not a literal place. It is a psychological and metaphysical landscape where sand symbolizes fragmented time — every grain a moment that has come loose from its proper sequence.
He reaches toward the glowing figure. He fails. He sinks into the sand. The sand pulls back and zooms outward, revealing itself to be the sand inside an hourglass. The scene transitions into childhood memory.
The audience does not yet understand what they are watching. That understanding is the story itself.

II. The Ashbourne Children’s Home
The Orphanage and Its Hidden Nature
The MC is a young orphan residing at The Ashbourne Children’s Home. He is curious, inwardly deep, psychologically sensitive, and already carrying something unusual — an innate capability that nobody around him has vocabulary for yet. He possesses a natural warmth, coherence, and depth that makes him quietly remarkable to anyone who spends time near him.
What appears to the outside world as a charitable institution for orphaned children is, in truth, a carefully constructed pipeline owned and operated by a secret Masonic cult. Its legal ownership is hidden behind fabricated names and false records. The cult uses the orphanage’s respectable public face to access, observe, and selectively acquire children who demonstrate unusual capabilities. Every child inside Ashbourne has already been identified and assessed before any formal action is taken.
The Three Miracles and Noam’s Deployment
A boy named Noam arrives at the orphanage. He is not an orphan. He was deliberately sent by his highest Masonic parents as an instrument of reconnaissance — deployed to locate and identify the secret weapon their organization has been searching for across generations: a child capable of yielding what they believe to be the key to fragmenting time itself.
Noam is the same age as the MC but built entirely differently. Groomed from birth into presentation and intimidation, he wears well-furnished clothes always kept immaculate, and has attended dedicated classes for walking, standing, and moving with authority. His first impression of the MC is quiet condescension: “What a poor fellow.” He sees an orphan beneath him. He has no idea he is looking at the most significant person he will ever meet.
Noam witnesses the first miracle privately. He says nothing, and waits. The second miracle occurs. Now he is consciously anticipating, something building inside him that his careful conditioning was never designed to contain. He expects the third miracle. But before it arrives, his immaturity cracks through his composed exterior. The thrill, the suspense, the sheer weight of witnessing something inexplicable breaks him open. He reports what he saw to his family.
The third miracle never occurs. The MC is publicly escorted into Noam’s family before it can happen. The cult’s machinery begins moving, now operating on two miracles and an assumption. They never see the full picture. They never will.
The Public Adoption
The adoption is presented through newspapers and media as an act of charitable kindness. The MC is photographed sitting beside his smiling friend, welcomed as a new son into a respected family. In reality this is the beginning of his exploitation. The cult has already formed agreements with scientists, and both parties intend to use the MC for their long-term goal: the fragmentation of time itself.
The MC’s foster family — the people who raised him before this adoption — signed their consent willingly. Their motivation was the promise of divine power. He was not lost to them through poverty or circumstance. He was surrendered as a transaction. He was currency.
An unknown mother — a widow of poverty — had sold one of her twin sons to the cult shortly after birth, receiving wealth in a letter crate bearing the cult’s markings. This twin was brought into Ashbourne’s pipeline. He would later die inside the facility during an experiment. His mother would spend years believing she simply made a desperate choice, never knowing what that place truly was. Her surviving son grew up beside her, carrying stuffs and chattering childishly, unaware his brother existed.

III. Alina — The Caretaker
Arrival and the Bond
Inside the cult’s facility, a young girl named Alina is hired as a caretaker for the children in residence. She is four years older than the MC. She comes from a respectable middle-income background, known across wealthy households for her discretion and trustworthiness. She wears a classic vintage black and white maid’s uniform — her passport and her invisibility cloak in that world. People see the uniform before they see her.
Among all the children she oversees, the MC stands out to her immediately. Not because anyone told her he was special, but because she felt it. His empathy, his inward coherence, his quiet depth anchored something in her she could not fully explain. She needed him as much as he needed her. The bond formed instantly and genuinely — peer-level despite the age difference, maternal in function given the era’s standards of maturity, and growing in complexity as both of them aged.
The cult noticed what they could measure. His experimental results stabilized around her presence. She became an instrument of yield optimization without ever knowing it. Every genuine moment between them was simultaneously someone else’s research data.
Resignation and the Garden
At a certain point, Alina was quietly resigned from her duties. No dramatic confrontation. An administrative decision. She was no longer needed in that capacity, or the cult decided her stabilizing effect had served its purpose. The MC, still a child, did not react outwardly. He received her absence with the same stillness he received her presence. But internally the first fracture formed — the first proof the world offered him that connection could be taken without warning. The emotional restraint and structured survival mask he would develop were built on the day she left.
Alina could not stay away. She secured a half-time position as a garden worker at the mansion — an excuse to exist in the same space as him. The MC was occasionally brought to the inner mansion garden for brief, unsupervised strolls. In those stolen moments Alina would approach carefully, terrified that being seen near him would reveal her defiance and bring consequences. Sometimes she risked it anyway. A gentle pat. A kiss on his forehead. Tears running down her face she could explain to no one.
The MC stood completely still. Received everything. Showed nothing outwardly. His stillness was its own act of love — he protected her by not reacting. Any visible display of their bond would have confirmed her defiance. His composure shielded her.
The News of Demise
Then the garden strolls stopped. He was no longer brought outside. Alina returned for a week, checking. Desperate, she pushed deeper into the facility than she had ever gone — into restricted laboratory compartments she had no clearance for. Through a corridor she was never meant to be in, wearing her uniform that made her functionally invisible to the hierarchy, she overheard that a boy from their facility had failed an experiment. Had not survived.
She did not know with certainty it was him. But she knew. She left. Carrying traces she was unaware of. Returning to her flat still in her uniform. The same black and white outfit that had given her access to him now just fabric in a quiet room while she fell apart. Her neighbors heard the intensity of her grief through thin walls. To them it was just another ordinary sorrow in the residence. Nobody knocked.
What she did not know — and would never know — was that the boy who died that day was not him. It was the other twin. The son sold to the cult in a letter crate by a desperate widow. A child who entered those walls through a transaction and did not survive them.
The Harbour and the Turning Point
Alina stood at a cliff near the harbour intending to end her life. She said to herself: “Why couldn’t I bring him home.” Not anger at the cult, not rage at the world — a verdict she passed on herself alone. A guilt built on incomplete information that she had no way of correcting.
On the edge, she saw a working woman struggling with a heavy load who slipped and fell. Her instinct activated before her grief could stop it. She rushed to help. While gathering fallen items, Alina herself slipped and fell into the water. The woman cried for help. Alina was pulled from the water by a young boy of the MC’s age. Through blurred, tear-soaked vision she saw his face — for one suspended moment, it was him. Then clarity returned and it was not. She held that stranger boy and wept. In the cold harbour water something settled: killing herself was never going to bring him home either.
She visited the woman afterward, learning she was the boy’s mother. During their conversation — after the woman sent her son outside to play — the woman revealed she had once sold a twin son to a rich family out of desperate poverty, receiving payment in an ornate letter crate. Alina inspected the crate. The markings were unmistakable. It belonged to the same Masonic family she had served. The same walls she had walked through in her uniform. She absorbed this truth in silence, thanked the woman, and left. She never returned. She would later piece together that the boy who died in the facility was this same twin. She carried that knowledge entirely alone, choosing never to burden that mother with a truth too dark to survive.
Alina’s Campaign
At eighteen, Alina underwent a transformation. She was now a blooming adult with age-authority to confront matters with little repulsion against her will. She carried insider knowledge of the cult’s operations, the ownership of Ashbourne, and the true nature of what happened inside those walls. She chose to act.
She built an underground information network from nothing. Beginning with pamphlets — small, careful, untraceable, each attributed to an entirely different anonymous name on a weekly rotating basis. She studied the patterns of secret news publishers. She formed connections individually. She wrote major articles covering the cult’s true nature and published them under anonymous impressions. She did not fear speaking truth even if it led her to the grave.
The cult, with all their money and geniuses and counterintelligence resources, could not locate the source. Each piece of information appeared to come from a different person. They sent troops in undercover forms — beggars, drunkards, middle-class citizens — to search every household. Nothing. They tracked secret publications, shut them down, interrogated workers. Nothing. Their public reputation began deteriorating.
Their suspicion turned inward — someone from their own domain had betrayed them. Still nothing concrete emerged.
The Ashbourne Fire and the Rescue
A great fire broke out in the Ashbourne Children’s Home. The fire was not accidental — it originated in a single targeted compartment, clearly an attempt to destroy specific evidence. But it spread beyond its intended scope, becoming a visible public event. Their attempt to erase evidence became the evidence.
Alina moved immediately. She led her assembled network of connections to the charity house, broke in, and rescued every child inside. Miraculously, no children were harmed. Alina and the rescuers all collapsed outside from smoke inhalation. As Alina lost consciousness, she saw a vision of the MC patting her head and kissing her forehead — the garden gesture returned to her in the space between waking and darkness.
For three days afterward, Ashbourne remained empty and unrepaired. No cult representatives appeared. No officials. Alina recognized the silence correctly — the cult had gone still, reassessing, aware that any visible presence would worsen their public situation. She did not enter. She understood the building would be watched from invisible positions. She waited.
The children returned on their own. Their home, their familiar space — they went back to collect what remained of their belongings from the rubble. Some of their temporary caretakers accompanied them. Whatever the targeted compartment had tried to destroy, fragments of it were now dispersed across dozens of temporary homes throughout the city. The cult watched it happen and could do nothing visible without catastrophic public consequence.
The Third Miracle Revealed
What became clear in this period — entirely unnoticed by Noam and the cult’s hierarchy — was that these Ashbourne children possessed unusual capabilities of their own. Each was a small echo of what the MC carried — a speckle of dust to his magnitude. They had not gathered and acted randomly.
The MC, at age fourteen while still inside the cult’s facility, had communicated with the children of his old orphanage on secret terms. This was the third miracle — not a supernatural display, not something observable and measurable, but a living connection maintained across distance and walls and surveillance through whatever innate quality made him fundamentally different. He reached them. They remembered. And when the moment came, they responded.
Alina’s physical effort rescued the children. But their subsequent movements — returning to collect evidence, dispersing it safely — were guided by him. Two networks operating in parallel without awareness of each other, converging on the same outcome.
Alina noticed the patterns. She could not explain them. She prayed every day that he was alright, and she dearly wished to meet him again.

IV. The First Escape
Two Years of Knowledge
Inside the facility, the MC had spent two years in a state of complete hidden awareness. The second miracle — defined in full below — allowed him to touch any book or document and absorb its complete contents in a fraction of time equivalent to a single sand grain falling through an hourglass. He had read their documents. He understood their theories, their crimes, their intentions, and his own nature with a clarity the cult never suspected he possessed.
He knew what they were. He knew what they had done. He remained their loyal, obedient specimen. Not from defeat. From patience. He was waiting for the one moment the first miracle would reveal.
The Hourglass Collection
Noam had noticed the MC’s obsession with hourglasses during this period. He observed him staring into an hourglass for an entire day and assumed he was counting sand grains as curiosity or passing time. What the MC was actually doing was perceptually quantifying time as a matter of observation and contemplation. To him, time was a completely different dimension than it appeared to others. His first miracle allowed him to read time’s movement with sufficient precision to predict with near-certainty what was most likely to occur hours ahead of its happening.
The hourglass was not an obsession. It was the physical object most analogous to what his consciousness naturally did. He collected them because they were the closest representation of what he actually was.
Six Minutes
After two years of watching, the MC identified a single fraction of possibility across his entire seventeen years of captivity — a moment when the facility’s human systems briefly created an unmonitored gap. He walked himself out. No violence, no elaborate plan, no dramatic escape. Just a young man moving through corridors with the measured calm of someone who knew exactly what each second would hold.
It took him six minutes to walk and run out of the facility’s region. It took three minutes after his departure for them to realize he was gone. By then he had already blended into the crowd of the outside world. If he had moved a second earlier or later, he would have failed.
The cult’s greatest specimen escaped not through power but through patience and precision. Their machines, their geniuses, their century of accumulated resources — circumvented by a young man who had learned to read time itself.
First Hours of Freedom
He ran to a nearby settlement and secured a room at a busy inn without cost — reading the situation well enough to navigate a transaction without money, without leaving a trail, without drawing attention. Then he slept for an entire week. His body claiming what seventeen years had stolen from it all at once. Not a choice. A systemic collapse of everything that had been running on survival instinct with nothing left to run on once the threat was momentarily removed.
He woke numb and completely dumbfounded. Not relieved. Not grateful. Just blank. Freedom, arriving after seventeen years of captivity, did not feel like anything recognizable at first. He had been an instrument so long he did not know what he was when nobody was playing him. He was seventeen years old, scarred in ways clothing could hide, with capabilities nobody suspected, sitting in an inn full of strangers with nowhere to be for the first time in his life.
His capabilities were effectively inaccessible in this state. They required a specific internal condition to function — not emotional vacancy, but calm groundedness. Not turbulence of any kind: not lethargy, not romantic feeling, not anger, not fear. In his destabilized condition he had nothing but ordinary human vulnerability.
Reunion at Ashbourne
Wandering the city silently — highly introverted, responding actively only when approached — he passed by The Ashbourne Children’s Home. He observed its emptiness. Standing before the place where his story truly began, he closed his eyes and, with careful precaution, reactivated the same silent communication of the third miracle he had used at age fourteen.
When he opened his eyes, a small crowd of young boys — roughly fifteen to sixteen years of age, the Ashbourne children now approaching maturity — were approaching him with expressions of wonder and amazement. They recognized not his face but the feeling. The specific quality of that silent communication had left an imprint deep enough that when it happened again, their feet moved toward it before their minds could question it.
They asked him many questions and surrounded him with the instinctive warmth of people who had been waiting for someone to return. They told him of an angelic woman who had led others to rescue them from a fire. The MC said quietly that this reminded him of Alina. The entire crowd went silent. Some of the boys had been raised by her after the fire. They confronted him: how did he know that name.
Before he could answer fully, she arrived.

V. The Reunion
Alina, now twenty-two years old, came to check on the boys she had raised. She saw him.
Not a ghost. Not a boy of his age pulling her from water. Not a phantom child glimpsed outside a building. Him. Actually him. Grown. 190 centimetres of someone she last saw as a restrained child standing still in a garden, receiving what little she could give him through fear and tears.
He moved first. Despite his introversion. Despite seventeen years of conditioned stillness. He crossed the distance and took her hands. Not an embrace. Not words. Just presence confirmed as real.
She broke quietly. The way Alina did everything — completely, without performance. She embraced him.
She held him with everything maternal — the relief of a woman who had said “why couldn’t I bring him home” and found him home anyway. He held her with pragmatic certainty — a man who had known for a long time what she was to him, too shy to name it, choosing to hold it quietly. Two people loving each other genuinely and completely in entirely different languages, neither saying the thing they most needed to say.
Alina adored him with maternal love and was too afraid to embrace the marital bond. The MC saw her as his companion — his love pragmatic and certain, his shyness too great to propose, his nature too careful to impose.
Over time, through a period of reunion left for later detailed documentation, this suspension resolved into something acknowledged by both. She stopped seeing the boy she could not bring home and recognized the man who came home anyway — a complete protection. He felt, for the first time in his life after wholeheartedly embracing her as his companion, an uttermost serenity. She became the mediator of his soul.
They formed an eternal bond. They guarded each other against all odds. Both held to the same boundary of purity in their bond — their love expressed through presence, patience, and protection rather than physical expression.

VI. The Recapture
The Cult’s Desperation
The cult, now in possession of a few fragile prototype samples of time fragments — the product of a century of plotting, rituals, and exploited potential — could not afford this loss. Without the MC, those samples were functionally incomplete. They could not replicate what they did not fully understand, and they had never fully understood it. Their search was conventional at first: undercover troops dispersed across the city dressed as beggars, drunkards, and middle-class citizens, conducting household-by-household searches without the technology to efficiently detect their target.
The MC’s first miracle made their movements predictable and avoidable. He sensed their patterns before they materialized. They could not find him through ordinary means.
So they used the fragmented time prototypes as a weapon against their own creator. The prototype samples were sufficient to generate blind spots in the MC’s perceptual quantification of time — moments he could not read, gaps in the probability stream where things happened outside his awareness. His own potential, however incompletely extracted, turned against him.
They did not use this to capture him directly. They used it to capture Alina.
He came. Without calculation. Without timing. Without the six-minute precision of his first escape. Just a man walking toward the people holding the mediator of his soul and placing himself in their hands. Submissively. Completely. Voluntarily. The mediator, the careful one, the man who effortlessly avoided hurting anyone — surrendered by his own nature.
Chosen Vacancy
Back inside the facility’s walls, the MC became empty again. Not because the experiments broke him immediately. But because he chose it. He had read their documents. He knew that emotional vacancy was the state their experiments required. He produced it himself, deliberately, as an act of protection. As long as he cooperated, Alina remained alive in custody. The cult believed they had recaptured their compliant instrument. They did not understand that a man who chooses vacancy is not the same as a man who has it forced upon him.
Alina in custody understood exactly what his submission cost him. That knowledge was its own specific torment.

VII. The Second Escape and the Breaking Point
Escape
At a point left for later detailed documentation, the MC and Alina managed to escape together. They were free. They found themselves facing something worse than captivity.
The Ashbourne Boys
The Ashbourne boys — those they had each built genuine bonds with across years, the ones the third miracle had reached, the ones Alina had raised toward maturity — were in the room. All of them tied to chairs. Showing twenty-four hours of continuous torture. Motionless enough that distinguishing the unconscious from the dead was impossible from where they stood.
Both the MC and Alina began losing consciousness from the overwhelming trauma of the sight. From behind them came an intimidating figure — the head authority of the cult and science group, the oath-keeper, who had sworn to ensure nothing of what happened there ever reached the outside world. From the exit came a figure Alina recognized as resembling the MC before she understood who it was.
Noam.
He approached nose to nose with the MC — cocky, extroverted, pissed but also annoyingly amazed by how mature and influential the MC had become. Deep beneath his composure, invisible sweat betrayed what his ideology refused to acknowledge: he was terrified. His body remembered something his mind had buried. Private military troops filed in behind him, forming a frontline. The oath-keeper’s damaged presence behind.
Noam spoke few harsh words. The MC’s anger — expressed for the first time as a metaphysical aura, a form of presence that destabilized the room without physical action — intensified into something that answered those words. He struck Noam with his bare forearm, sending him into the frontline. An amateur soldier’s panic pulled a weapon trigger. The bullet found Alina.
Alina’s Death
Before her head reached the floor, he crossed an impossible distance — held from both sides, far from her, against every physical measure — and caught her whole in his arms.
She did not give him her pain. Even now. She absorbed this too, and gave him a smile instead. Her hand rose to his cheek. The garden gesture reversed — her palm against the face of the man she could not bring home who came home anyway.
Her final words were not goodbye. They were instructions. She told him: do not let yourself down no matter what. Stand for good and justice. Put an end to evil. Do this as obligation — the sacred duty of someone gifted as he was gifted, done for the sake of the greater reward that obligation returns. And through all of it, remain yourself. Do not let your shadow form overtake you.
She named the shadow in her final breath. The thing she feared most for him was not his enemies. It was the version of him that vacancy produced — the form the cult had engineered and she had always stood between him and. With her last words she drew a line between him and it.
She departed peacefully.
He placed both of her hands on her chest. Then he stood up. The viewer cannot see his face. But everyone who witnessed what followed felt what it meant before it happened.
The scene cuts to aftermath: the entire room of trained military personnel down, either faint or dead. The oath-keeper on his knees, dragging himself toward a door on damaged knees. The MC standing in the center, panting, eyes completely red with intensified blood flow.
He had placed her carefully before the shadow came. He had heard her final instruction. He chose the shadow anyway. Because the alternative — facing that room as only himself — felt insufficient for what justice required. That contradiction will define everything that follows.
The Shot and the Aftermath
Carrying Alina in his arms, heading for the exit, the MC heard a weapon fire. He saw blood draining from his waist. His vision blurring, he could make out a figure holding a weapon — face unidentifiable through fading clarity. Before losing consciousness, he gently placed Alina on the ground. Then he fell.
The figure with the weapon was Noam. He had regained consciousness during the shadow form’s aftermath — surrounded by fallen troops, the oath-keeper crawling — and waited. He chose the moment when the shadow was spent, when the MC’s back was turned, when dizziness had already set in. He shot him in the waist. Not the head. Not the heart. Whether this was strategic calculation — the specimen still needed alive — or whether something older and buried stayed his hand in that final second, only Noam knows.
The oath-keeper arrived in a wheelchair with facility reinforcers. He assessed the scene: the MC in critical condition, the fallen maid, Noam laughing uncontrollably — his first exposure to fragmented time having produced a complete crack in his composed exterior. The oath-keeper issued quiet disposal instructions for Alina and loud urgent medical instructions for the MC. He had Noam brought to him by the neck, thrown to the ground, and threatened: if Noam’s bed-sick father heard of this, the heir’s path to the throne would be delayed ten more years. The chaotic laughter stopped instantly. An amusedly disgusted expression. An eye twitch. The composure attempting to reassemble over something that could no longer fully hold it.

VIII. The Tombstone
The MC woke in his old room inside the facility. He went outside without hesitation, without submissiveness, without any of the conditioned compliance that had once defined his movements in that space. He found the old garden — the garden where she had kissed his forehead through tears — now bearing a newly constructed platform. A tombstone.
He read the name. Alina.
He went to his knees. He placed his hands on the tombstone as if they were on her shoulders and released every fragment of grief he had been carrying. He cried like a child until unconsciousness took him on her grave.
He woke in a newly constructed room with new equipment and newly installed gadgets. He was inside two straitjackets. The claustrophobic trauma activated immediately into anger. A scientist — one of the many innocent researchers forced into the cult’s service through contractual agreement — came to comfort him. He told the MC it would all be alright. The MC stared into him. The scientist nodded and attempted to maintain his sanity with few quiet words.
The cult referred to the MC as their soul of existence.

IX. The Final Phase of Experimentation
The Time Fragment Suction Chamber
The MC was moved through several procedure phases before being brought to the time fragment suction chamber — the primary apparatus through which his potential was to be extracted as usable time fragment resources. Initial test results were poor. The cult identified that he was at his weakest spot: without Alina, without anchor, without the specific internal stability his capabilities required.
They had tricks remaining. At the climax of one procedure session, new chambers were unveiled before him while he underwent the abstract suction process at his weakest. The chambers had been concealed with cloth. They were unveiled one by one.
In each chamber: a dead Ashbourne boy. The children he had contacted through the third miracle at age fourteen. The children who had approached him with wonder outside the abandoned orphanage. The children Alina had raised. Strangled. Gone.
His emotional erosion at the sight yielded surplus resources of a kind the instruments had rarely recorded. Chamber after chamber unveiled. He recalled ten boys. There was an eleventh chamber. He did not possess curiosity for it anymore — only exhaustion and anguish. He was never removed from the straitjackets again from this point. The cult was thoroughly familiar with his shadow form.
He was drained completely for one week. Noam encountered him afterward — sometimes hostile, sometimes passive-aggressive, always demonstrating through these interactions that he had chosen to rot his core completely for the cult’s agenda and had fully absorbed their ideology as his own identity.
The Eleventh Chamber
The following week, the MC resisted again. This was the day the cult needed to reach a priceless surplus of time fragments and could not delay further. Noam took control of the experiment personally. He presented himself as professional despite the amateur quality beneath the surface. He never turned to face the MC directly during procedures — a silent demonstration of both his ego and his terror.
After two hours of procedure yielding nothing, Noam began taunting the MC. The shadow form began to surface — the red eyes, the altered expression, the physical tells of something other than the man himself emerging. Noam waited for the climax. Then he unveiled the eleventh chamber.
Inside: Alina’s fresh corpse, preserved and displayed.
The MC went into full berserk mode. The potential yielded exceeded anything previously recorded. But within that yielding, the two forms began to fluctuate simultaneously — his original self and his shadow self in direct, irreconcilable conflict. The original soul — the one that had placed her hands on her chest, that had communicated with children through warmth and connection, that had chosen vacancy to protect her — recognized the sin and the blasphemy of what was being done. The shadow form sought obliteration. Every instrument in that room was measuring something the cult had never measured before.

X. The Oscillation of Eras
The fluctuation between the two forms at maximum potential density was the true trigger. Not the experiment succeeding — but two irreconcilable versions of the same soul pulling at the fabric of reality in opposite directions simultaneously, at the meaning density only Immaculate Thought could generate.
Noam had ordered maximum pressure. The scientists had warned against it. His need for vengeance and his absolute absorption into the cult’s ideology overrode every caution.
The Oscillation of Eras occurred.
Time fragmented. Reality destabilized. Different historical eras collided spatially. Existence became permanently desynchronized. The facility transformed into a decayed, distorted structure suspended in temporal disarray. All cult scientists and personnel on-site were killed. The world was altered irreversibly.
The catastrophe was not caused ultimately by the cult’s century of ambition. It was caused by one man’s refusal to lose. The boy whose single moment of childlike excitement had delivered the MC to this place ended everything with a single order driven by wounded pride.
The Oscillation of Eras cannot be undone. Time cannot be rewound or stabilized. The narrative world permanently exists in altered synchronization. Nothing will be restored.

XI. The Desert — Understood
The desert returns. Now the audience understands it completely.
The glowing entity the MC crawls toward is himself — the child he was before everything. Full of curiosity and wonder. The original whole state before the cult’s erosion, before the experiments, before the vacancy, before the fission. The child who once found an hourglass, opened it, and saw a vision from a different perspective before Noam pulled him away by the shirt with the words: “Behave. Put the lid back.”
The Hope Entity was never external salvation. It was always internal reconnection. Not a person to be rescued by. Not a world to be restored. The MC reaching toward himself — the version that existed before seventeen years of systematic destruction — and this time, unlike the opening attempt, succeeding.
He connects. The world remains broken. Nothing is restored. The Oscillation of Eras is permanent. He no longer sinks.
The story ends suspended there: not with recovery, but with acceptance. Preserving what remains after the end of everything. The soul that adapted rather than restored. The moral continuity that survived catastrophic fragmentation. Hope as integration, not salvation.


“The phenomenon is irreversible. The story does not center on restoration. It centers on adaptation and moral continuity in a broken reality.”

project-zaman/narrative/summary.title: Summary
project-zaman/narrative/summary.content:
PROJECT ZAMAN
Narrative Summary
Project Zaman is a dark metaphysical tragedy about a gifted orphan known as the MC, whose natural connection to time makes him the target of a secret Masonic cult. The story explores trauma, memory, emotional survival, exploitation, and the meaning of hope in a reality that can no longer be restored.
At its core, the story is not about fixing the past.
It is about surviving after irreversible damage.

1. Core Premise
The MC is an orphan raised in The Ashbourne Children’s Home, a place that appears to be a charitable orphanage but is secretly operated by a powerful Masonic cult.
The cult uses Ashbourne to identify children with unusual abilities. Among all the children, the MC is the most extraordinary. He possesses a rare metaphysical connection to time, making him the key to the cult’s ultimate goal:

The fragmentation of time itself.

Through manipulation, false adoption, scientific exploitation, and spiritual abuse, the cult turns the MC’s gift into a weapon. But his story is not only about power. It is about the people who try to protect his humanity, especially Alina, the caretaker who becomes the emotional anchor of his soul.

2. Opening Image: The Desert and the Hourglass
The story begins with a surreal image.
The MC crawls through an endless desert toward a glowing figure. The desert is not a real location. It represents a broken psychological and metaphysical state, where every grain of sand symbolizes a fragment of time.
The MC reaches toward the glowing figure but fails. He sinks into the sand.
The scene then pulls outward, revealing that the desert was actually the sand inside an hourglass.
This opening does not make sense at first. Its meaning becomes clear only near the end of the story.

3. The Ashbourne Children’s Home
The MC grows up in The Ashbourne Children’s Home, unaware that the orphanage is part of a hidden cult operation.
The cult studies orphaned children and selects those who show unusual abilities. The MC is identified as the most valuable child among them.
A boy named Noam is sent to the orphanage by his powerful Masonic family. He is not an orphan. He is a planted observer, sent to locate the child the cult has been searching for.
Noam witnesses two of the MC’s miracles and reports them too early. Because of this, the cult takes action before understanding the full nature of the MC’s abilities.
The MC is publicly adopted by Noam’s family under the appearance of charity. In reality, this adoption marks the beginning of his captivity and exploitation.

4. Alina: The Caretaker and Soul-Mediator
Inside the cult’s facility, the MC meets Alina, a young caretaker who is four years older than him.
Alina immediately senses something different in him. His warmth, empathy, silence, and emotional depth affect her deeply. Their bond forms naturally and sincerely.
To the cult, Alina becomes useful because the MC’s experimental results stabilize around her presence. Without knowing it, she becomes part of their research system.
To the MC, however, she becomes something far greater.
She becomes his emotional anchor.
She becomes the person who helps him remain human.

5. Separation and Alina’s Transformation
Alina is eventually removed from her caretaker role. The MC does not react outwardly, but internally, this becomes one of his first deep emotional fractures.
Unable to stay away, Alina returns as a garden worker just to exist near him. Their meetings become quiet and secret. She sometimes risks approaching him, giving him small gestures of affection, while the MC remains still to protect her from being discovered.
Later, Alina hears that a boy from the facility has died in an experiment. She believes it was the MC.
This nearly destroys her.
At the edge of ending her life, she is interrupted by an accident at the harbour. She survives and eventually learns that the dead boy was actually another child connected to the cult’s hidden operations.
This revelation transforms her grief into purpose.
Alina begins exposing the cult through anonymous writings, pamphlets, and underground publications. She builds a hidden information network and becomes one of the cult’s greatest unseen enemies.

6. The Ashbourne Fire and the Third Miracle
The cult attempts to destroy evidence by setting fire to a part of Ashbourne Children’s Home. The fire spreads and becomes a public disaster.
Alina leads a rescue operation and saves the children.
Later, it becomes clear that the Ashbourne children themselves possess small traces of unusual ability. They are connected to the MC through what is revealed as his third miracle.
The third miracle is not a dramatic supernatural display. It is a silent connection across distance, memory, and time.
At age fourteen, while still inside the facility, the MC had secretly communicated with the children of Ashbourne. When the right moment came, they responded.
Alina rescued them physically.
The MC guided them silently.

7. The First Escape
After years in captivity, the MC escapes the cult facility.
He does not escape through violence.
He escapes through patience, observation, and precision.
His ability allows him to read the movement of time with extreme accuracy. After watching the facility for years, he identifies one perfect gap in their system.
He walks out.
The escape takes six minutes.
The cult realizes he is gone three minutes later.
By then, he has already disappeared into the outside world.

8. Reunion with Ashbourne and Alina
After escaping, the MC eventually returns to Ashbourne and reconnects with the boys from the orphanage.
They recognize him not by appearance, but by the familiar feeling of his silent communication.
They tell him about an angelic woman who rescued them from the fire. The MC realizes they are speaking about Alina.
Then Alina arrives.
She sees him alive.
Not as a ghost.
Not as a memory.
Not as the child she failed to save.
But as the man who survived.
Their reunion is the emotional heart of the story. Alina embraces him with maternal love, while the MC sees her as his companion and the mediator of his soul.
Their bond becomes pure, protective, and eternal.

9. Recapture and Alina’s Death
The cult cannot allow the MC to remain free. They use incomplete time-fragment prototypes to create blind spots in his perception.
Instead of capturing him directly, they capture Alina.
The MC surrenders himself voluntarily to save her.
Later, during another escape attempt, the MC and Alina discover the Ashbourne boys tied to chairs after brutal torture. The sight nearly breaks them both.
Noam appears, now fully consumed by the cult’s ideology.
A confrontation follows. The MC’s anger manifests as a terrifying metaphysical presence. In the chaos, a soldier fires a weapon.
The bullet hits Alina.
The MC catches her before she falls.
In her final moments, Alina tells him to stand for good, fight evil, and remain himself. Most importantly, she warns him not to let his shadow form overtake him.
Then she dies peacefully in his arms.

10. The Shadow Form
After Alina’s death, the MC breaks.
He places her carefully down, then gives in to the shadow form — the darker version of himself created by trauma, vacancy, experimentation, and grief.
The aftermath is devastating.
The room of soldiers is left destroyed. The MC survives, but the act marks a major contradiction in his soul:
He heard Alina’s warning.
He understood it.
And still, he chose the shadow.
This becomes one of the defining conflicts of the story.

11. The Tombstone
The MC wakes inside the facility again.
He goes outside and finds the old garden, where Alina once secretly comforted him.
There, he sees a tombstone with her name.
He collapses at her grave and cries like a child until he loses consciousness.
This moment shows the full weight of his grief. The person who kept him emotionally alive is gone, and the world around him continues to treat him as an object.
The cult now refers to him as their soul of existence.

12. Final Experimentation
The cult enters its final phase of experimentation.
They place the MC inside a time-fragment suction chamber to extract the maximum amount of usable temporal energy from him.
When the results are weak, they use emotional destruction as a method.
They reveal chambers containing the dead Ashbourne boys.
Then, in the eleventh chamber, they reveal Alina’s preserved corpse.
This breaks the MC completely.
His original self and shadow self begin to conflict at maximum intensity. One side recognizes the horror and sin of what is happening. The other seeks total destruction.
The cult’s instruments record something beyond anything they have ever seen.

13. The Oscillation of Eras
Noam, driven by pride, hatred, and desperation, orders the experiment to continue under maximum pressure despite warnings.
This causes the catastrophe known as:

The Oscillation of Eras

Time fractures permanently.
Different historical eras collide.
Reality becomes desynchronized.
The facility transforms into a decayed temporal ruin.
The world itself is permanently altered.
The Oscillation cannot be undone.
Time cannot be restored.
The story’s world is now broken forever.

14. Ending: The Desert Understood
The story returns to the desert.
Now the audience understands what it means.
The glowing figure the MC was crawling toward was never an outside savior.
It was himself.
More specifically, it was the child he used to be before captivity, trauma, experiments, vacancy, and grief.
The MC reaches toward his original self.
This time, he connects.
The world is not fixed.
Alina does not return.
The dead remain dead.
Time remains broken.
But the MC no longer sinks.

15. Main Themes
Time as Trauma
Time is not just a supernatural system in the story. It represents memory, grief, patience, loss, and psychological fragmentation.
The broken world reflects the broken inner state of the MC.

Love as an Anchor
Alina is not simply a caretaker or love interest.
She is the person who keeps the MC connected to his humanity. Her presence stabilizes him emotionally, spiritually, and metaphysically.

Exploitation of Innocence
The cult treats gifted children as tools, resources, and experiments. The story strongly criticizes systems that disguise cruelty behind charity, science, religion, and power.

Self vs Shadow
The MC’s greatest enemy is not only the cult.
It is the version of himself created by suffering.
His shadow form represents what happens when pain becomes identity.

Hope as Integration
The ending does not offer restoration.
Instead, it offers integration.
The MC cannot undo what happened, but he can reconnect with the part of himself that survived it.

16. One-Line Summary
Project Zaman is a tragic metaphysical story about a time-gifted orphan exploited by a secret cult, anchored by love, shattered by loss, and forced to survive in a permanently broken reality where hope means reconnecting with the self rather than restoring the past.

project-zaman/narrative/themes.title: Themes
project-zaman/narrative/themes.content:
Project ZAMAN is built on four interlocking themes. None of them stand alone — each one depends on the others to mean what it means. Together they form the philosophical architecture of the world.


01 — Adaptation Over Restoration
The core principle. The Irreversibility Principle made thematic.
The world of Project ZAMAN cannot be fixed. The Oscillation of Eras is permanent. Alina is dead. The original MC no longer exists as a unified being. The 11th Chamber has been opened. None of these things can be undone — not by power, not by will, not by the completion of any quest or the defeat of any antagonist.
This is the theme that defines the game’s relationship to the Soulslike genre. Where many Soulslikes present the player with a broken world and task them with restoring a previous order — lighting the fire, ending the cycle, reclaiming the throne — Project ZAMAN refuses that structure. There is no previous order worth restoring. The cult’s exploitation of Immaculate Thought was always going to produce this. The Oscillation was not an accident to be corrected. It was a consequence to be lived with.
Subject-001’s arc enacts this theme directly. He does not spend the narrative trying to reverse the fission or resurrect the original MC. He spends it learning how to exist as a fragment in a fractured world — adapting to what he is rather than mourning what he was.
The question this theme asks: When return is impossible, what does moving forward actually mean?

02 — Hope as Integration
The answer to the first theme. What adaptation looks like from the inside.
Hope in Project ZAMAN is not optimism. It is not the belief that things will improve or that the world can be made right. It is something more structural and more demanding: the capacity to carry the whole self forward — including its broken parts — without the broken parts becoming the only thing that defines it.
The Hope Entity embodies this theme literally. It is the original MC’s childhood self, preserved in the Desert before the system reached him. Reconnecting with it is not regression — it is integration. Subject-001 does not return to innocence. He incorporates the unfractured self into his present, fractured one. He becomes someone who contains his own full history rather than being destroyed by it.
This theme also runs through Alina’s final instruction. She does not tell Subject-001 to fix the world, or to avenge her, or to restore what was lost. She tells him to stay himself. That instruction is a definition of hope: the self persisting, coherent, carrying its values forward into a world that tried to erase them.
The question this theme asks: What remains possible when nothing can be restored?

03 — Identity Under Systematic Erasure
The theme that runs beneath everything. What the cult is actually doing.
The cult — Anthropos publicly, Gibborim privately — is not merely exploiting Immaculate Thought. It is engaged in a systematic project of identity erasure. It names its subjects in Hebrew. It numbers them. It extracts them from the contexts that formed them — families, bonds, histories — and reinserts them into a framework where they are defined entirely by their function to the order.
The original MC resists this not through defiance but through existence. He cannot be named by the system because he was never given a name it could absorb. He carries miracles that require the internal calm of a self the system could not fully reach. His bond with Alina — chosen, voluntary, outside institutional structure — is precisely the kind of connection the cult cannot classify or contain.
Subject-001 inherits this resistance. His gradual discovery of his own origin is simultaneously a recovery of identity: learning who he was before the number, before the fracture, before the system decided what he was for. The Hope Entity is the purest expression of this theme — the self before erasure, waiting to be reclaimed.
Noam is the theme’s shadow. He is what systematic formation produces when there is no resistance: a person so thoroughly shaped by the cult’s identity framework that the question of who he might have been has become unanswerable.
The question this theme asks: What survives of a self that a system spent years trying to replace?

04 — The Cost of Innocent Harm
The theme carried by Noam. What the narrative refuses to simplify.
Noam reported the original MC’s miracles out of childlike excitement. He was not calculating. He was not cruel in that moment. He was a child doing what he had been shaped to do — seeking approval, sharing something remarkable, performing the function his parents had prepared him for without fully understanding that it was a function at all.
The consequences of that innocent act are total. The extraction. The cult’s access to the MC. The years of exploitation. The Oscillation. Alina’s death. Every fracture in the narrative traces a line back to a child who was excited and did not know what he was doing.
Project ZAMAN does not use this to exonerate Noam. His subsequent decay — from condescension to cruelty to full ideological capture — is his own, built on choices made with increasing awareness of what the system is. But it refuses to make him a simple villain. He is the product of a formation that began before he could consent to it, executing a harm he did not intend, and spending the rest of the narrative becoming the kind of person who would intend it.
This theme also complicates Subject-001’s relationship to Noam. The antagonist is not a stranger. He is the person whose excitement — innocent, childlike, unaware — set everything in motion. Confronting him is not straightforward. It never was.
The question this theme asks: When harm begins in innocence, where does responsibility actually begin?

How the Themes Interact






























ThemeEnacted ByCounterpointAdaptation over restorationSubject-001’s arc, the Irreversibility PrincipleThe cult’s fantasy of controlled restoration through Immaculate ThoughtHope as integrationThe Hope Entity, Alina’s final instructionThe shadow form — vacancy as the alternative to integrationIdentity under systematic erasureThe original MC’s namelessness, Subject-001’s discoveryNoam — fully erased, the system’s success storyThe cost of innocent harmNoam’s formation and decaySubject-001 — what the same system failed to fully produce

The themes do not resolve into answers. They resolve into a posture: eyes open, self intact, continuing.
